title: Managing Call-Outs in the Classroom
author: Jonathan Nicolas Jarrett-Kerr
summary: Jarrett-Kerr argues that the common teacher response to a student calling out an answer -- praising the correct answer while gently reminding them not to call out next time -- actively reinforces the behavior rather than curbing it, because the dopamine hit of being right and acknowledged lands before the correction and quietly rewards the very thing the teacher is trying to stop. His preferred script, borrowed from Adam Boxer, is to state plainly 'In this classroom, we don't call out,' break eye contact deliberately, and re-ask the question to the room, without extended discussion or public correction, dealing with the behavior in the moment without handing the student the validation they were seeking. He goes further upstream, recommending that teachers frontload the participation instruction into the question itself (e.g., 'Without calling out, what plant part absorbs water?' rather than tacking the instruction on afterward), so the expectation is set before the temptation to call out even arises. Jarrett-Kerr frames managing call-outs as an equity issue, not just a classroom-management tactic: letting the loudest or fastest students answer first systematically silences quieter students who have the answer but never get the chance, and teaching students to wait and contribute within a structure is itself a transferable communication skill valued by employers. He closes with a companion scenario -- a student who won't answer at all -- and argues both extremes (over-answering and under-answering) are really about the same underlying decision a teacher must make about how participation works in the room.
points: Jarrett-Kerr's central behavioral-science claim is that praising a correct call-out ('Well done, John, correct. But next time, don't call out.') backfires because the dopamine reward for being right arrives before the correction, reinforcing the exact behavior the teacher wants to eliminate.

His preferred intervention, credited to Adam Boxer, is a short scripted response -- state the norm, break eye contact, re-ask the question to the room -- that handles the behavior in the moment without giving the student public validation.

He recommends frontloading participation instructions into the question itself (stating the constraint before the question rather than after) so the expectation is set before the temptation to call out ever arises, eliminating the need for correction entirely.

He frames call-out management as an equity issue: allowing the fastest or loudest students to answer first systematically silences quieter students who know the answer but never get the chance to give it.
quotes: The most common answer I hear is what I call the soft approach: a quiet word in the student's ear... And this approach does work. But it has a problem, and the problem is timing.

The dopamine arrives before the correction, and so the wrong message arrives in the form of dopamine. This dopamine hit will verify that shouting out works. This fatal validation of the shout-out via praise doesn’t curb the behaviour. It encourages it.

Even better, we can do what Adam Boxer calls frontloading the means of participation, so instead of “What plant part absorbs water? Without calling out!” try “Without calling out, what plant part absorbs water?” One small shift in word order, and the expectation is set before anyone has had a chance to call out.

Allowing students to call out is an equity issue. If we let the loudest voices answer first, we are sending a message: the quickest gets heard. I am far more interested in the quiet voice at the back.

If every teacher lets a student call out whenever the answer comes to mind, that student is never going to learn how to communicate in a way that works in a group. Teaching them to wait, to listen, to contribute within a structure is teaching them a genuinely useful skill.
Getting participation right is one of the most important ways of ensuring that you have an equitable classroom.
